question: Fitting in the workshop is best defined as…
options: Removing metal with a rotating multi-point milling cutter
Joining two parts permanently by melting them together
Shaping, finishing and assembling parts by hand tools to accurate size
Coating parts with a thin electro-deposited metal layer
explanation: Fitting is manual bench work: shaping, finishing and assembling components with hand tools to accurate dimensions.

question: Fitting work is normally done with the job held in a…
explanation: Fitting achieves accuracy by filing, sawing, drilling and tapping, usually with the job in a bench vice.

question: Which operations are typical of fitting (bench work)?
explanation: The fitting lecture lists filing, sawing, drilling and tapping as the means of achieving accuracy.

question: Why is fitting still taught when CNC machines exist?
options: It needs no measuring tools or drawings at all
It completely replaces every machining process
It is faster than CNC for every kind of job
It builds manual precision for prototyping, repair and maintenance
explanation: Fitting teaches manual precision before automation and is needed in prototyping, maintenance and R&D.

question: Which skill is the fitting lab mainly meant to develop?
options: CNC part programming with G and M codes
Dimensional accuracy, tolerance awareness and surface finishing
explanation: The fitting lecture lists precision handwork, tolerance control, surface finishing and tool control.

question: Which of these is NOT a fitting (bench-work) operation?
explanation: Fitting operations: marking, sawing, chipping, filing, scraping, drilling, tapping and dieing. Knurling is a lathe operation.

question: Which is a real-world application of manual fitting given in the fitting lecture?
options: Fitting turbine blades and repairing gear housings
Mass-producing bolts on a CNC lathe
explanation: Aerospace, automotive, tool design and defence: e.g. fitting turbine blades, repairing shafts and gear housings.

question: How many main types of fit are there?
options: Four: clearance, press, shrink and slide
explanation: The fitting lecture: mainly three types — clearance, interference and transition.

question: In a clearance fit, the shaft is…
options: Always larger than the hole, needing force
Always smaller than the hole, giving free movement
explanation: Clearance fit: shaft smaller than hole, free movement (e.g. a shaft rotating in a bearing).

question: In an interference fit…
options: The shaft is slightly larger, so force is needed to assemble
There is always a large gap between the parts
No assembly is possible at all between the parts
The shaft is smaller, so it rotates freely inside
explanation: Interference fit: shaft slightly larger than the hole, pressed in (e.g. a gear pressed onto a shaft).

question: A fit in which the tolerance zones overlap, giving either a slight clearance or slight interference, is a…
explanation: Transition fit: conditional overlap, a light push fit.

question: A gear pressed onto a shaft so that it cannot slip is an example of…
explanation: The fitting lecture gives "gear pressed into shaft" as the interference-fit example.

question: What material is used for the ME-106 fitting job?
explanation: The fitting lecture states the material is mild-steel plate, as per the workshop drawing.

question: In the ME-106 fitting tasks, to what accuracy is the metal block filed in Task 1?
explanation: Task 1: file a metal block to exact dimensions (±0.1 mm), to understand sawing and filing.

question: Which ME-106 fitting task is meant to "prepare for assembly"?
explanation: Task 3: drill and tap a hole — prepare for assembly.

question: What is the final task (Task 4) of the ME-106 fitting lab?
explanation: Task 4: assemble and inspect fit — the final project.

question: Task 2 of the ME-106 fitting lab — creating a square/triangle shape — mainly develops…
explanation: Task 2: create a square/triangle shape — accuracy with files.

question: What is the stated objective of the ME-106 fitting lab?
options: Learn CNC programming of a milling machine
Learn to cut spur gears on a milling machine
Learn laser cutting of thin metal sheet
Learn manual accuracy and verify dimensions with measuring tools
explanation: Objective: learn manual accuracy and verify dimensions with measuring tools.

question: Which tools are listed for the ME-106 fitting lab?
options: Grinding wheel, dresser, magnetic chuck, coolant, parallels
Wire electrode, dielectric supply, clamping wire, power supply
Hacksaw, files, hammer, try square, centre punch, Vernier, bench vice
Index plate, mandrel, catch pin, worm wheel, tailstock
explanation: The fitting lecture lists hacksaw; flat, round, half-round, triangular and square files; hammer; try square; centre punch; Vernier caliper; bench vice.

question: In fitting, the bench vice is used to…
explanation: Bench vice — holds the workpiece firmly.

question: In fitting, the hacksaw is used for…
explanation: Hacksaw — rough cutting of metal.

question: In fitting, files are used for…
explanation: Files — smooth finishing and shaping.

question: What is a try square used for?
explanation: Try square — ensures 90° accuracy of edges and surfaces.

question: In the fitting lab, the centre punch is used for…
explanation: Centre punch — for layout and marking, especially drill points.

question: According to the fitting lecture, the hammer is used for…
explanation: Hammer — used for chipping and shaping.

question: Which tools are used for precise measurement in the fitting lab?
explanation: Vernier caliper / steel rule — for precise measurements.

question: Which of these is NOT a part of a bench vice?
explanation: Bench vice: fixed jaw, movable jaw, jaw plates, screw, handle, body/slide and base. The tang is part of a file.

question: Why are soft (copper or aluminium) jaw caps fitted over the vice jaws?
options: To make the jaws grip the job much harder
To conduct heat away from the job quickly
To protect finished surfaces from the serrated jaws
To measure the size of the job directly
explanation: The vice jaws carry hardened, serrated plates; soft caps prevent marks on finished work.

question: When holding a job in a vice for filing, it should project…
options: Only a little above the jaws, to avoid vibration
Far above the jaws for easy access
Well below the jaws, hidden inside
At an angle of 45° to the jaws
explanation: Keeping the job low in the vice prevents it from springing and chattering.

question: A tool with a V-groove used to hold round bars while marking or drilling is a…
explanation: V-blocks hold cylindrical work steady.

question: Which holding device is used to hold very small jobs or drills in the hand?
explanation: Pin vices hold small round jobs/drills; hand vices hold small jobs in the hand. C-clamps clamp work to a table.

question: An L-shaped block used to hold work at 90° to the surface plate is an…
explanation: An angle plate has two faces at 90°.

question: A surface plate provides…
options: A true flat reference surface for marking and checking flatness
A sharp hardened edge for scribing lines
A magnetic surface for holding steel jobs
A graduated scale for measuring lengths
explanation: The surface plate (cast iron, granite or hardened steel) is the flat datum for marking out and checking flatness.

question: Surface plates are commonly made of…
explanation: Surface plates are made of cast iron, granite or hardened steel.

question: A hardened steel pointed tool used to scratch lines on metal is a…
explanation: The scriber scribes lines for marking out.

question: Which tool scribes lines parallel to the surface plate at a set height?
explanation: The surface gauge (marking block) carries a scriber on an adjustable pillar.

question: Which tool, with one bent leg and one pointed leg, is used to draw lines parallel to an edge?
explanation: Odd-leg calipers also find the centre of round bars.

question: Which tool is used to draw circles and arcs on metal?
explanation: A divider has two pointed legs; it draws circles/arcs and transfers distances.

question: The point angle of a dot punch is about…
explanation: Dot punch ≈ 60° (light witness marks); centre punch ≈ 90° (deeper drill-start mark).

question: The point angle of a centre punch is about…
explanation: A centre punch has a 90° point to make a deeper mark for locating the drill.

question: How does a dot punch differ from a centre punch?
options: Dot punch (60°) makes light witness marks; centre punch (90°) makes a deeper drill mark
Dot punch (90°) makes deep drill marks; centre punch (60°) makes light marks
Dot punch is used only on wood
explanation: Witness marks along scribed lines use the 60° dot punch; drill points are marked deeper with the 90° centre punch.

question: Which instrument is used for precise marking and height measurement from a surface plate?
explanation: The Vernier height gauge combines a scriber with a Vernier scale.

question: Before scribing lines on a metal surface, it is often coated with…
explanation: Chalk or marking blue makes the scribed lines clearly visible.

question: A steel rule can measure to an accuracy of about…
explanation: A steel rule reads to about 0.5 mm; a Vernier to 0.02 mm; a micrometer to 0.01 mm.

question: The least count of a typical Vernier caliper is…
explanation: Typical Vernier calipers have a least count of 0.02 mm.

question: The least count of a Vernier caliper is equal to…
options: The length of the Vernier scale
One main-scale division plus one Vernier division
One main-scale division minus one Vernier division
explanation: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = (value of 1 MSD) ÷ (number of Vernier divisions).

question: A Vernier has 50 divisions that span 49 main-scale divisions of 1 mm. What is its least count?
A Vernier has 10 divisions equal to 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm. What is its least count?
The reading of a Vernier caliper is…
options: Main-scale reading + (coinciding Vernier division × least count)
Main-scale reading − least count of the Vernier
explanation: Total = MSR + (k × LC).

question: Which of these can a Vernier caliper NOT measure directly?
explanation: A Vernier caliper measures outside (outside jaws), inside (inside jaws) and depth (depth rod).

question: Which part of a Vernier caliper is used to measure the depth of a hole?
explanation: The depth rod slides out from the end of the beam.

question: The least count of a metric outside micrometer is…
explanation: Pitch 0.5 mm ÷ 50 thimble divisions = 0.01 mm.

question: A micrometer screw has a pitch of 0.5 mm and the thimble has 50 divisions. What is the least count?
explanation: LC = pitch / divisions = 0.5 / 50 = 0.01 mm.

question: The reading of a micrometer is…
explanation: Total = sleeve (mm + 0.5 mm if visible) + thimble division × LC.

question: Which part of a micrometer ensures a uniform measuring pressure?
explanation: The ratchet slips at a set torque so every reading is taken at the same pressure.

question: Which of these is NOT a part of a micrometer?
explanation: Micrometer parts: frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve (barrel), thimble, ratchet, lock nut. A depth rod belongs to a Vernier caliper.

question: Outside and inside calipers are read by…
options: Counting thimble divisions on the leg
Transferring the setting to a steel rule
Reading a dial fitted on the hinge
explanation: Plain calipers transfer a size; they have no scale of their own.

question: A Vernier caliper shows a reading of 25.36 mm. When its jaws are closed, it reads +0.04 mm (positive zero error). What is the correct reading?
explanation: Correct reading = observed − positive zero error = 25.36 − 0.04 = 25.32 mm.

question: A micrometer reads 12.47 mm. With the faces closed it reads −0.02 mm (negative zero error). What is the correct reading?
explanation: A negative zero error is added: 12.47 + 0.02 = 12.49 mm.

question: Which part of a hacksaw is used to tension the blade?
explanation: The wing nut on the frame tightens the blade to the correct tension.

question: How should a hacksaw blade be fitted in the frame?
options: Teeth pointing back towards the handle
Teeth pointing forward, away from the handle
explanation: The hacksaw cuts on the forward stroke, so the teeth must point forward.

question: When sawing with a hacksaw, pressure is applied…
options: Never; the saw cuts by its weight
explanation: The fitting procedure: apply pressure only on the forward stroke; release it on the return.

question: For cutting a thin-walled tube, which hacksaw blade should be chosen?
explanation: Fine-pitch blades keep at least 2–3 teeth on thin or hard sections; coarse pitch suits soft thick material.

question: Hacksaw blades are generally made of…
explanation: Blades are hardened high-carbon steel or HSS.

question: Which part of a file fits into the wooden handle?
explanation: File parts: tang, heel, face, edge, point. The tang goes into the handle.

question: Files are classified by…
options: Length, grade of cut, cross-section and type of cut
Speed of use and length of handle
explanation: Files are specified by length, grade (cut), cross-sectional shape and single/double cut.

question: Arrange file grades from COARSEST to FINEST.
options: Rough → bastard → second cut → smooth → dead smooth
Dead smooth → smooth → second cut → bastard → rough
Bastard → rough → smooth → second cut → dead smooth
Second cut → rough → bastard → dead smooth → smooth
explanation: Rough is coarsest; dead smooth is finest.

question: Which file grade is used for fast metal removal (rough work)?
explanation: Bastard files remove metal quickly; smooth and dead-smooth files give the final finish.

question: Which file would you use to finish an internal corner of less than 90°?
explanation: Triangular files reach acute corners; round files enlarge holes; flat files do flat surfaces.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Fitting lecture s.8

question: Which file is used for filing a concave curved surface and also a flat surface?
explanation: The half-round file has one flat side and one curved side.

question: Which file is used for filing large flat surfaces?
explanation: The fitting procedure: flat file for flat surfaces, round/half-round for curves.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Fitting lecture s.12

question: Files are made of…
explanation: Files must be hard to cut steel, so they are hardened and tempered high-carbon steel.

question: Draw filing is done to…
options: Give a fine finish by pushing the file sideways along the work
Cut a narrow slot in the job with the file tip
Mark a line on the job with the file edge
Remove metal quickly by filing across the work
explanation: Cross filing removes metal; draw filing (file held crosswise, moved along the work) gives a fine finish.

question: Filings that clog the teeth of a file (pinning) are removed with a…
explanation: A file card is a wire brush for cleaning file teeth.

question: The cutting angle of a flat cold chisel for mild steel is about…
explanation: For mild steel the chisel point is ground to about 60°.

question: Taps are used to cut…
explanation: Taps cut internal threads; dies cut external threads.

question: In what order are the taps of a set used?
options: Bottoming tap → intermediate (second/plug) tap → taper tap
Bottoming tap → taper tap → intermediate (second/plug) tap
Intermediate (second/plug) tap → bottoming tap → taper tap
Taper tap → intermediate (second/plug) tap → bottoming tap
explanation: The taper tap starts the thread, the intermediate tap deepens it, and the bottoming tap cuts full threads to the bottom of a blind hole.

question: A tap is turned using a…
explanation: A tap wrench turns the tap; a die stock holds and turns a die.

question: What tap-drill size is used for an M10 × 1.5 thread?
explanation: Tap drill ≈ major diameter − pitch = 10 − 1.5 = 8.5 mm. (This is a drilling rule of thumb leaving some thread engagement; the lathe formula Dc = D − 2 × 0.6134p gives the full core diameter.)

question: What tap-drill size is used for an M8 × 1.25 thread?
explanation: Tap drill ≈ 8 − 1.25 = 6.75 mm (a 6.8 mm drill is used).

question: Before drilling a hole in fitting, the drill point is first…
options: Filed flat with a smooth file
Centre-punched so the drill does not wander
explanation: A centre-punch mark guides the drill point and stops it slipping.

question: Which hammer is most used in fitting?
explanation: The ball-peen hammer (flat face + ball peen) is the usual fitting hammer.

question: The hemispherical end of a ball-peen hammer is used for…
explanation: The ball peen spreads metal for riveting and peening; the flat face is for striking.

question: In a cross-peen hammer, the peen is…
options: Wedge-shaped and at right angles to the handle
Wedge-shaped and parallel to the handle
explanation: Cross peen: at right angles to the handle. Straight peen: parallel to the handle.

question: Fitting hammers are specified by…
explanation: Hammers are specified by head weight (e.g. 0.25–1 kg) and are forged carbon steel.

question: What is the FIRST step of the ME-106 fitting procedure?
options: Cutting along the lines with a hacksaw
Safety check, then clamp the work firmly in the vice
Filing the edges with a flat file
explanation: Step 1: safety check — apron and goggles, tools in good condition, workpiece clamped firmly in the bench vice.

question: In the ME-106 fitting procedure, which tools are used for marking?
options: Steel rule, scriber and try square
explanation: Step 2: mark dimensions using the steel rule and scriber; use the try square to keep 90° edges.

question: Why are punch marks made at drill points (step 3 of the fitting procedure)?
options: To harden the metal at that point
To measure the hole depth later
To file the edge more easily
To prevent the drill bit from slipping
explanation: Step 3: light hammer blows make punch marks at drill points; purpose: prevent the drill bit from slipping.

question: Which step comes immediately AFTER centre punching in the ME-106 fitting procedure?
options: Cutting along the marked lines with a hacksaw
Marking with scriber and try square
explanation: Order: safety → marking → centre punching → cutting → filing → checking → fitment & inspection.

question: In the filing step of the ME-106 procedure, how should the file be moved for a smooth finish?
explanation: Step 5: use the flat file for flat surfaces and round/half-round for curves; maintain uniform motion.

question: What is done in the "checking" step of the ME-106 fitting procedure?
options: Polish with emery paper and pumice powder
Plate the job with a thin layer of nickel
Harden the job in a furnace and quench it
Measure with Vernier and try square; re-file if necessary
explanation: Step 6: measure with Vernier/try square to ensure accuracy; re-file if necessary.

question: What is the LAST step of the ME-106 fitting procedure?
options: Fitment and inspection by the instructor
explanation: Step 7: assemble and check the fit; submit the piece for the instructor's inspection.

question: What is the correct sequence of the ME-106 fitting procedure?
options: Safety check → marking → centre punching → cutting → filing → checking → fitment & inspection
Safety check → cutting → marking → filing → centre punching → fitment & inspection → checking
Marking → safety check → cutting → centre punching → checking → filing → fitment & inspection
Centre punching → marking → safety check → filing → cutting → checking → fitment & inspection
explanation: The seven steps from the fitting lecture.

question: In the fitting procedure, why is marking done BEFORE cutting?
options: Marking is optional and can be done later
Marking hardens the metal along the line
The cutting and filing must follow the marked lines
The hacksaw needs chalk on the job to cut
explanation: Marking (scriber, rule, try square) sets out the lines that the saw and files then follow.

question: Which precaution about the bench vice is given in the fitting lecture?
options: Keep the jaws loose for easier filing
Keep the jaws tight and parallel; clamp the job securely
Hammer the vice handle to tighten it fully
Never use a vice for holding any job
explanation: Keep bench vice jaws tight and parallel and clamp workpieces securely.

question: What should be done with damaged hand tools?
options: Use them only for rough work
explanation: Do not use damaged tools; keep tools sharp and properly gripped.

question: Which precaution about force is given for filing and sawing?
options: Use your body weight on the return stroke
Strike the file with a hammer
Apply maximum force on both strokes
explanation: Excess force breaks blades, spoils the finish and causes injury.

question: Why must a file never be used without a handle?
options: The file will bend in use
The pointed tang can pierce the hand
explanation: Never use a file without a handle — the tang can injure the palm.

question: How should filings be cleared from the bench?
options: By wiping them off with the bare palm
By leaving them on the bench for later
With a brush, not by blowing or with bare hands
By blowing them away with the mouth
explanation: Blowing sends particles into eyes; bare hands get splinters.

question: Which is correct practice when sawing with a hacksaw?
options: Use steady, full-length strokes with correct blade tension
Press hard on the return stroke as well
Twist the blade in the cut to steer it
Use short fast strokes with a loose blade
explanation: Use the full blade length, steady strokes and correct tension; ease off near the end of the cut.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Fitting lecture s.12

question: Which tool is UNSAFE to use?
options: A sharp scriber with a cap
A file with a tight handle
A chisel with a mushroomed head
A hammer with a firm head
explanation: A mushroomed chisel head can throw off splinters; a loose hammer head can fly off.

question: Which of these is a fitting-shop precaution from the lecture?
options: Work without goggles for better view
Keep filings on the bench for reuse
Maintain a clean and safe workspace
explanation: A clean workspace is one of the listed precautions.

question: The fitting-lab safety motto is…
explanation: From the fitting lecture safety slide.

question:
Assertion (A): A hacksaw blade is fitted with its teeth pointing away from the handle.
Reason (R): A hacksaw cuts on the forward stroke.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both true, and R explains A.

question:
Assertion (A): A centre punch is used before drilling.
Reason (R): A centre punch has a 60° point angle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: A is true, but R is false: a centre punch is about 90°; the dot punch is about 60°.

question: A try square is used to measure diameters to 0.02 mm.
explanation: False. A try square checks squareness (90°); diameters to 0.02 mm are measured with a Vernier caliper.
ref: Fitting lecture s.9; Theory: Hajra Choudhury

question: A micrometer has a finer least count than a Vernier caliper.
explanation: True: 0.01 mm vs 0.02 mm.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Fixed jaw. Stationary jaw cast with the body.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Movable (sliding) jaw. Moves in and out on the slide when the handle is turned.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Jaw plates. Hardened, serrated plates screwed to the jaws that grip the work.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Screw (spindle). Square-threaded screw that moves the movable jaw.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Handle (tommy bar). Turned to tighten or loosen the vice.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Body / slide. Guides the movable jaw.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Base. Bolted to the work bench.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Workpiece. Job gripped between the jaws, projecting only a little above them.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled C?
options: Hardened, serrated plates screwed to the jaws that grip the work
Stationary jaw cast with the body
Square-threaded screw that moves the movable jaw
explanation: C = Jaw plates. Hardened, serrated plates screwed to the jaws that grip the work.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled D?
options: Hardened, serrated plates screwed to the jaws that grip the work
Square-threaded screw that moves the movable jaw
Job gripped between the jaws, projecting only a little above them
explanation: D = Screw (spindle). Square-threaded screw that moves the movable jaw.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled B?
options: Job gripped between the jaws, projecting only a little above them
Turned to tighten or loosen the vice
Moves in and out on the slide when the handle is turned
Hardened, serrated plates screwed to the jaws that grip the work
explanation: B = Movable (sliding) jaw. Moves in and out on the slide when the handle is turned.
label: B

question: Which tool is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Scriber. Scratch (scribe) fine lines on metal for marking out.
label: A

question: Which tool is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Try square. Check squareness (90°) of edges and surfaces.
label: B

question: Which tool is shown in panel C?
explanation: C = V-block. Hold round bars steady for marking or drilling.
label: C

question: Which tool is shown in panel D?
explanation: D = Surface gauge (scribing block). Scribe lines parallel to the surface plate at a set height.
label: D

question: Which tool is shown in panel E?
explanation: E = Odd-leg (jenny) caliper. Draw lines parallel to an edge or find the centre of a bar.
label: E

question: Which tool is shown in panel F?
explanation: F = Divider. Draw circles and arcs, and transfer distances.
label: F

question: Which tool is shown in panel G?
explanation: G = Angle plate. Hold work at 90° to the surface plate.
label: G

question: Which tool is shown in panel H?
explanation: H = C-clamp. Clamp work to a table or angle plate.
label: H

question: Which panel shows the surface gauge (scribing block)?
explanation: D = Surface gauge (scribing block). Scribe lines parallel to the surface plate at a set height.
label: D

question: Which panel shows the odd-leg (jenny) caliper?
explanation: E = Odd-leg (jenny) caliper. Draw lines parallel to an edge or find the centre of a bar.
label: E

question: Which panel shows the angle plate?
explanation: G = Angle plate. Hold work at 90° to the surface plate.
label: G

question: Which punch is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Dot punch. Point angle about 60°; light witness marks along scribed lines.
label: A

question: Which punch is shown in panel B?
explanation: B = Centre punch. Point angle about 90°; deeper mark to locate the drill.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Frame. Holds the blade in tension.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Blade. Hardened saw blade (high-carbon steel or HSS) with teeth.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Handle. Gripped to push and pull the saw.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Wing nut. Tightens the blade to the correct tension.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Teeth. Point forward, away from the handle, because the saw cuts on the forward stroke.
label: E

question: In the hacksaw figure, in which direction must pressure be applied?
explanation: The teeth (E) point away from the handle, so the saw cuts and is pressed only on the forward stroke.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Fitting lecture s.12

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Tang. Pointed end that fits into the wooden handle.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Heel. Uncut part next to the tang.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Face. Broad cutting surface carrying the teeth.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Edge. Narrow side of the file.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Point (tip). Far end of the file, opposite the tang.
label: E

question: Which file shape is shown in cross-section A?
explanation: A = Flat file. Filing flat surfaces.
label: A

question: Which file shape is shown in cross-section B?
explanation: B = Square file. Filing square slots and holes.
label: B

question: Which file shape is shown in cross-section C?
explanation: C = Round file. Enlarging round holes and filing concave curves.
label: C

question: Which file shape is shown in cross-section D?
explanation: D = Half-round file. Filing concave curves (round side) and flat surfaces (flat side).
label: D

question: Which file shape is shown in cross-section E?
explanation: E = Triangular (three-square) file. Filing corners and angles less than 90°.
label: E

question: The file in section C is mainly used for…
options: Filing concave curves (round side) and flat surfaces (flat side)
Filing corners and angles less than 90°
Enlarging round holes and filing concave curves
explanation: C = Round file. Enlarging round holes and filing concave curves.
label: C

question: The file in section E is mainly used for…
options: Enlarging round holes and filing concave curves
Filing corners and angles less than 90°
explanation: E = Triangular (three-square) file. Filing corners and angles less than 90°.
label: E

question: The file in section D is mainly used for…
options: Filing concave curves (round side) and flat surfaces (flat side)
Filing corners and angles less than 90°
explanation: D = Half-round file. Filing concave curves (round side) and flat surfaces (flat side).
label: D

question: Which hammer is shown in panel A?
explanation: A = Ball-peen hammer. Flat face for striking; hemispherical peen for riveting and peening.
